"Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one.
kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; \"copies\" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; \"other\" otherwise.
meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: It removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations or solver iterations), so that those steps are computed at the same time. Running independent copies side by side, or splitting each single step across GPUs, does not count.
Give for each a quote from the proposal and a reason of at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Problem:
Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models for river catchments, which needs long MCMC chains.
Proposals: [{\"index\":1,\"bottleneck\":\"Wall-clock to a target effective sample size is set by the serial autocorrelation time of one chain. Running K independent chains in parallel replicates burn-in K times and yields the same posterior more precisely but no faster per unit of new information; more GPUs buy more of the same samples.\",\"assumption\":\"Calibration must be one or a few long independent chains exploring the exact posterior by local (random-walk or crossover) moves.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the unit of work from a chain to a population: parallel-tempered replicas or an SMC sampler with 10^3-10^4 interacting walkers on GPU. Each mutation step is embarrassingly parallel across the population, and swap/resample steps replace long serial traversals of correlated, multimodal parameter directions with population-level mixing, converting serial mixing time into parallel breadth.\",\"question\":\"Across ~20 CAMELS catchments with GR4J/HBV (8-14 parameters), does a GPU parallel-tempering or SMC sampler with 1024-4096 replicas reach ESS=1000 in >=20x less wall-clock than a tuned DREAM-ZS chain, at equal error on posterior quantiles? Measured: wall-clock to ESS target and quantile error vs an overnight reference chain.\",\"measure\":\"Cheapest test: lumped model at ~1 ms per likelihood, so the whole study fits one GPU. Implement 16-32 temperatures x 64-128 walkers (JAX/blackjax or custom), 20 catchments, compare wall-clock to ESS=1000 and to reference quantiles from a long DREAM run. Cost: ~2-3 weeks engineering + <$50 GPU. Kill criterion: <5x advantage on the hardest, most multimodal catchments means the serial bottleneck was never real.\",\"compute_after\":\"Wall-clock stays flat as the population grows until the GPU saturates, then scales across GPUs. Extra compute buys more temperatures (higher swap acceptance) and more particles (lower SMC variance), i.e. shorter time-to-answer and better tail exploration rather than more identical samples.\",\"exact\":\"Yes. Replica-exchange and SMC samplers are asymptotically exact for the same posterior; no likelihood approximation is introduced.\",\"expected\":\"Large gains (10-100x wall-clock) exactly where rainfall-runoff posteriors are multimodal/strongly correlated from equifinality (threshold and exchange parameters); little gain on easy near-Gaussian posteriors, where DREAM already mixes in ~10^4 steps.\",\"fails_if\":\"Posteriors are unimodal and cheap to mix so there is no serial bottleneck to remove; or likelihoods are so cheap that kernel-launch and swap-synchronization overhead eats the gain; or the true blocker is an expensive distributed forward model, which this does not touch.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Parallel tempering / replica-exchange MCMC (Geyer 1991; Earl & Deem 2005); SMC samplers (Del Moral, Doucet & Jasra 2006); DREAM/DREAM-ZS (Vrugt et al.) as the hydrology incumbent; emcee (Foreman-Mackey 2013) and GPU population-MCMC practice in astronomy.\"},{\"index\":2,\"bottleneck\":\"Every catchment, event set, or climate scenario pays the full serial chain from scratch: cost = datasets x chains x steps x likelihood cost. For regional studies over thousands of catchments this multiplies a cost that GPUs cannot shorten because the chain is serial.\",\"assumption\":\"The posterior must be recomputed independently per dataset by iterative evaluation of the exact likelihood.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the objective from per-dataset chains to amortized inference: precompute one large bank of (parameter, simulated hydrograph) pairs fully in parallel, train a neural posterior estimator once, and get per-catchment posteriors in seconds. If exactness is required, use the learned posterior only as a proposal/preconditioner inside short delayed-acceptance chains with the true likelihood.\",\"question\":\"Does neural posterior estimation trained on <=2x10^5 simulations reproduce reference MCMC parameter marginals (Wasserstein distance <10% of posterior std) and posterior-predictive coverage (90% intervals covering 88-92% of held-out flows) across >=50 unseen catchments, including high-flow regimes? Measured: marginal distances, simulation-based calibration rank histograms, predictive coverage.\",\"measure\":\"Lumped-model test first: 2x10^5 GR4J simulations at ~1 ms each is minutes-hours on one node (<$50); train a small normalizing-flow NPE with the sbi toolkit (~1 GPU-day); validate against long reference chains on 50 catchments. Total ~2-4 weeks, <$500. The expensive variant (distributed model, ~5 min/run) needs ~10^6 core-hours, $3k-8k of cloud; run it only if the lumped test passes. If amortization fails even on the cheap smooth model, stop.\",\"compute_after\":\"All serial cost moves into the embarrassingly parallel simulation bank plus one training run; more compute linearly improves surrogate fidelity and tail coverage, and per-catchment inference cost no longer scales with chain length at all.\",\"exact\":\"No for pure NPE (approximate posterior). Exactness is recoverable via delayed-acceptance or importance reweighting with the true likelihood on a small final set of samples.\",\"expected\":\"For lumped models with smooth parameter-to-flow maps, marginals match within a few percent; weakest in extreme-flow regimes underrepresented in the prior bank and when the error model (Box-Cox + AR(1) residuals) dominates posterior shape but is absent from the training simulator.\",\"fails_if\":\"Catchments differ enough in data length, missing records, error structure, and regime that one amortized model underfits and per-case retraining costs more than just running DREAM; then nothing is saved.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Simulation-based inference / NPE (Papamakarios & Murray 2016; Lueckmann et al. 2017; Cranmer, Brehmer & Louppe 2020; sbi toolkit); GP and polynomial-chaos emulators used with SWAT-class hydrologic models; delayed-acceptance MCMC (Christen & Fox 2005); adjacent hydrology practice of LSTM-based parameter regionalization (Kratzert et al.).\"},{\"index\":3,\"bottleneck\":\"For spatially distributed rainfall-runoff models with 10^2-10^3+ gridded parameters, random-walk proposals shrink with dimension and required chain length grows roughly like d^2, so at any budget the chain never mixes; simultaneously each likelihood costs minutes to hours. More GPUs only buy more of a non-converged chain.\",\"assumption\":\"Inference must use derivative-free proposals (Metropolis, DREAM) on a black-box forward model.\",\"reframe\":\"Change what is measured from likelihood values to gradients: reimplement the model in a differentiable framework (or derive its adjoint) and use HMC/NUTS, with ensemble Kalman inversion as a gradient-light fallback. A gradient moves all parameters coherently, so the chain length needed for a given ESS stops scaling like d^2, and the expensive forward run is amortized over one informative step instead of one blind one.\",\"question\":\"For a distributed catchment model at d~50 and d~500: (a) is the measured adjoint gradient cost <=4x one forward run with checkpointing, and (b) does HMC's wall-clock-to-ESS=200 advantage over DREAM-ZS grow with d as predicted? Measured: gradient-cost ratio, ESS/hour for both samplers at both dimensions, 5 catchments.\",\"measure\":\"Cheapest version: a differentiable conceptual-distributed model (EXP-HYDRO / differentiable-HBV style, JAX or PyTorch) is a 2-4 week build; run NUTS (NumPyro/blackjax) vs DREAM at d=50 and d=500 on 5 catchments, one GPU, days of runtime, <$200. Kill criteria: adjoint cost >10x forward even with checkpointing over ~10^4 timesteps, or HMC fails to beat DREAM at d=500.\",\"compute_after\":\"GPU parallelizes forward/adjoint passes over space and forcing batches and runs many leapfrogs; each added unit of compute now attacks a chain whose required length grows slowly with d, so compute converts into reachable dimension (calibrating parameter fields previously uncalibratable) instead of more samples of the same low-dimensional posterior.\",\"exact\":\"HMC with Metropolis correction is exact MCMC for the same posterior; adjoint gradients are exact to floating point. The EKI/EnKS fallback is approximate (Gaussian-ensemble) and should be labeled as such.\",\"expected\":\"Adjoint at 2-4x forward cost with checkpointing; HMC advantage modest at d~10 (DREAM is fine there) and orders of magnitude at d~500. Main risk is memory over long time series, handled by sqrt-step checkpointing. Note the store dynamics are contractive, which keeps adjoints stable over long horizons.\",\"fails_if\":\"The posterior is discontinuous or stiffly multimodal (threshold parameters, rain/no-rain switching) so HMC trajectories stall and adaptation fails; or the production model is non-differentiable legacy code whose rewrite cost exceeds any plausible sampling gain.\",\"closest_prior\":\"HMC/NUTS (Neal 2011; Hoffman & Gelman 2014); differentiable hydrologic modeling and differentiable parameter learning (Shen et al.; EXP-HYDRO lineage); adjoint/4D-Var calibration tradition in land-surface and meteorological data assimilation; ensemble Kalman inversion (Iglesias, Law & Stuart 2013) as the derivative-free comparator.\"}]

This is the classic "reframe" that removes sequential dependency — e.g., converting a serial time-stepping simulation into something where steps can be computed simultaneously (like Picard iteration vs direct solve, or parallel-in-time methods, or swapping a serial iterative solver for a direct method).

In proposal 1: the MCMC chain's iterations still depend on each other step after step. So for proposal 1: kind = "reframe" (it changes what is computed/sampled — the algorithm and mixing structure — so more compute buys shorter time-to-answer, not more identical samples; compute_after explicitly says "shorter time-to-answer and better tail exploration rather than more identical samples"). meets_criterion = "no" (chain iterations still run sequentially; the population is parallel within each step, and walkers are coupled but iterations aren't computed simultaneously).

"so that those steps are computed at the same time" — the serial traversal steps (the steps the chain needed to take to traverse the space) are now effectively computed at the same time by different walkers?

Hmm, that's more like "replacing serial steps with a better step" than "computing steps at the same time." Like replacing an iterative solver with a direct method — that does remove solver iterations. Hmm, it IS kind of running many chains side by side, but coupled.

The reframe reduces T dramatically (mixing time) and increases information per iteration (population). But the step-after-step dependency is not removed — steps are not computed at the same time.

Wait, but actually — hmm, is that entirely true? Consider: with K independent chains (the bottleneck description), you run K chains side by side, each serial. The answer waits on the longest chain. With PT with K replicas: still K chains running side by side over T iterations, with swaps. The wall-clock is T iterations × cost per iteration (parallel across replicas). - kind: reframe / copies / other
- meets_criterion: yes / no / NA (for criterion about removing step-after-step dependency so steps are computed simultaneously)
